what_it_measures: How often the product team deploys to production in a calendar month. A DORA core metric — high frequency signals small-batch delivery and low release risk.
how_calculated: Direct count entered manually by EM/team. No formula — it is the raw value as-is.
null_behavior: Metric is skipped; its 30% weight redistributes to the other available metrics in Delivery Velocity.
known_limitations: Definition of 'deployment' varies across teams (some count environment promotions, others count production pushes only). Not auto-collected — relies entirely on EM discipline to fill in monthly. Teams with continuous deployment pipelines may under-report.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Confirm whether each team counts the same thing as a 'deployment'. Check if months with null values were intentionally skipped or simply forgotten.

what_it_measures: Average number of merge requests per human engineer who committed in the month. Proxy for throughput — how much work is being delivered in reviewable, mergeable units.
how_calculated: total_MRs_merged_this_month ÷ total_unique_human_contributors_this_month. Bot accounts are excluded from contributor count using a hardcoded list + regex patterns (e.g. *-bot, gitlab-runner, etc.).
raw_data_inputs: Per-repo JSON → mrs.total (MR count) and commits.active_contributors_human (bot-filtered). Aggregated across all active repos for the product.
scoring_window: Monthly (MRs merged in the calendar month; contributor count from same month's commits)
null_behavior: Returns null only if zero humans committed (e.g. no repo data collected). Redistributes its 35% weight.
known_limitations: Does not normalise for MR size or complexity — many tiny hotfix MRs score the same as fewer substantial feature MRs. Monorepos where all work lands in one large MR are systematically disadvantaged. Bot filter may miss custom CI bots not in the predefined list.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Spot-check: pick one repo, count MRs in the GitLab UI for the month, verify it matches the json value. Check if bot accounts were correctly excluded (look at per_contributor field in JSON).

what_it_measures: Number of features or user-facing deliverables shipped in the month. Captures business output beyond just code activity.
how_calculated: Uses manual value if provided. If null, falls back to count of unique JIRA ticket IDs referenced in commit messages across all repos (regex match on e.g. ENG-123, DISC-456). Fallback is a rough proxy only.
raw_data_inputs: Primary: manual-YYYY-MM.yaml → features_shipped. Fallback: per-repo JSON → tickets.unique_count (summed across repos).
elite_range: 30–60 features (capped at 100 score for values above 60)
null_behavior: If manual is null AND no ticket references found → metric skipped, 20% weight redistributes.
known_limitations: The auto fallback (ticket references) is unreliable: teams with poor commit hygiene under-count; teams that reference the same ticket in many commits over-count. The manual value requires subjective judgment about what counts as a 'feature'. Very small products (e.g. products with 5–10 devs) hit Elite easily, making cross-product comparisons misleading without context.
what_to_verify_in_qa: For months with non-null manual values: confirm the number is plausible given the cycle commitments. For months using the auto fallback (input_valid=OK but data_source=manual_or_auto): check if ticket references in the JSON seem realistic.

what_it_measures: Percentage of commits that are purposeful and structured — classified as feature, bugfix, or test work. High score means engineers write descriptive, intentional commits vs. noise (WIP saves, merge commits, tooling churn).
how_calculated: (feature_commits + bugfix_commits + test_commits) ÷ total_commits × 100. Classification is done per-commit using LLM analysis of commit messages (with heuristic fallback).
raw_data_inputs: Per-repo JSON → commit_classification.feature, .bugfix, .test, .maintenance, .tooling, .docs, .other. Aggregated across all repos.
null_behavior: Returns null if no commits were classified (no commits in month). Weight redistributes.
known_limitations: Classification quality depends on commit message quality. Teams with a culture of writing good commit messages score better regardless of actual work quality. Merge commits, auto-generated commits, and bot commits inflate the 'other' category and reduce the score. The 55% Elite threshold means a team can still score Elite with 45% non-intentional commits.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Look at a repo's raw commit_classification breakdown — do the category proportions match what you'd expect from that team's workflow? A team with 80%+ 'other' likely has poor commit discipline or classification is failing.

what_it_measures: Percentage of deployments that caused a rollback. A DORA core metric — measures how often changes break production.
how_calculated: rollbacks ÷ deployment_frequency × 100. Both inputs must be non-null and deployment_frequency must be > 0, otherwise returns null.
null_behavior: If either rollbacks or deployment_frequency is null → metric skipped, its 40% redistributes. Since deployment_frequency is rarely filled in, this metric is almost always null.
known_limitations: Depends entirely on consistent rollback reporting AND deployment tracking — if deployment_frequency is null (which it usually is), this metric can never be computed. 'Rollback' is inconsistently defined: some teams count feature flags disabled, others count only full git reverts. A team that never rolls back because they never fix production issues would score Elite — same as a team that never breaks production.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Check whether rollback count in the YAML aligns with incident records. Most months this will be null/MISSING — that is a data gap to flag to the EM, not necessarily a data error.

what_it_measures: Percentage of shipped features that generated a post-release defect (bug reported after deployment). Measures escaped defect density.
how_calculated: post_release_defects ÷ features_shipped × 100. Returns null if features_shipped is null/0 or post_release_defects is not provided.
raw_data_inputs: manual-YYYY-MM.yaml → post_release_defects (integer). Features_shipped from the same computation path described above.
null_behavior: Skipped if inputs missing. Its 35% weight redistributes to rework_rate (the only other available quality metric), which then carries the full quality component.
known_limitations: Definition of 'post-release defect' is subjective — does it include P2 bugs? Customer-reported only? Also depends on features_shipped being accurate. When the ticket fallback is used for features_shipped (instead of manual), the defect rate becomes unreliable. Currently almost never filled in.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Same issue as change_failure_rate: this is almost always null. Flag months where features were clearly shipped but this field is empty.

data_source: auto (GitLab MR classification preferred; git commit fallback)
what_it_measures: Percentage of meaningful work (feature + bugfix MRs or commits) that is rework/bugfixes rather than new feature work. High rework rate signals that previously shipped work is generating bug debt.
how_calculated: bugfix_MRs ÷ (feature_MRs + bugfix_MRs) × 100. Prefers MR-level classification; falls back to commit-level when MR classification is unavailable. Returns null if no feature/bugfix work was recorded.
raw_data_inputs: Per-repo JSON → rework_rate.percentage (already computed during collection). Aggregated across repos by re-computing from rework_rate.bugfix_count and rework_rate.feature_plus_bugfix sums.
null_behavior: Null if no feature/bugfix-classified work exists in the month (e.g. purely maintenance work). When the two manual quality metrics are also null, rework_rate carries the entire 30% Delivery Quality component alone.
known_limitations: Classification accuracy is the key risk: if commit/MR messages are vague ('fix', 'update', 'changes'), everything may land in 'other' and the metric returns null. Teams that do code review-driven rework (which is healthy) score the same as teams that ship bugs to production repeatedly. MR-level vs commit-level fallback can produce significantly different results.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Check the rework_rate.source field in the raw JSON — is it 'mr' or 'commit'? MR-level is more reliable. Compare the bugfix/feature split in commit_classification vs mr_classification for the same repo.

what_it_measures: Median number of days from when a feature is started (first commit or PR open) to when it reaches production. A DORA core metric — measures flow efficiency.
how_calculated: Direct manual input by EM. No formula — the EM provides the median across deployments for the month.
null_behavior: Almost always null in current data. Its 55% weight redistributes to cycle_delivery_accuracy, which then carries the full Efficiency component.
known_limitations: Hardest DORA metric to collect without dedicated tooling (e.g. LinearB, Swarmia). Start date is ambiguous (first commit? ticket created? sprint start?). Not auto-collected. The 55% weight means missing this metric has the single largest individual impact on any component score.
what_to_verify_in_qa: For any months where a value IS present, verify the definition of start/end dates used. Cross-check against cycle length — if cycles are 6 weeks, a lead time of 2 days is implausibly low.

what_it_measures: Percentage of cycle-committed items that were actually delivered by cycle close. Measures planning accuracy and team reliability.
how_calculated: cycle_items_delivered ÷ cycle_items_committed × 100. Includes a confidence weight: if committed < 15 items, the score is down-weighted proportionally (committed/15). Carry-forward: if no cycle closed this calendar month, the system looks back up to 2 prior months for cycle data.
raw_data_inputs: manual-YYYY-MM.yaml → cycle_items_committed and cycle_items_delivered (integers). Also cycle (C1, C2, ...) and optional cycle_carried_forward flag.
scoring_window: Per-cycle (6-week cycles), carried forward into the month the cycle closes
null_behavior: Null only if both current and 2 prior months have no cycle data. When lead_time_days is also null, this carries 100% of Engineering Efficiency.
known_limitations: Cycle boundaries (6 weeks) don't align with calendar months, so the month a cycle 'belongs to' depends on when it closed. Carry-forward means December data might show November's cycle — this is intentional but can confuse month-over-month comparisons. The confidence down-weight helps but small cycles (3–4 items) are still noisy. 'Item' definition varies: some teams count epics, others count stories.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Check the cycle field matches the expected cadence (C1→C2→C3 sequentially). Verify carry-forward months are flagged correctly. For very high scores (>90%), confirm the committed count is plausibly ambitious — easy commitments inflate accuracy.

what_it_measures: Average time in hours to restore service after a P0 or P1 incident. A DORA core metric. Only P0+P1 incidents are included — P2 (minor degradations) are excluded from MTTR calculation.
how_calculated: Average of (resolved_at – detected_at) in hours for all P0+P1 incidents in the month. Imported automatically from an incidents CSV export via import-incidents-csv.py.
raw_data_inputs: manual-YYYY-MM.yaml → mttr_hours (float). Also incidents.sev1, .sev2, .sev3 (counts, informational only — not used in scoring). The MTTR value itself must be computed externally before import.
concerning_range: 12–48 hours (value above 48h is treated as capped at max Concerning score)
null_behavior: If no P0/P1 incidents occurred, mttr_hours is null — metric is skipped. Its 40% weight redistributes to bus_factor and knowledge_distribution. Paradoxically, zero-incident months score better because the worst-scoring metric is absent.
known_limitations: Null in months with no P0/P1 incidents — this is correct behaviour but creates a scoring asymmetry: a team that had one severe incident and resolved it in 6 hours scores worse than a team that had no incidents. MTTR above 48 hours is scored as 0 (Concerning floor) — extreme values are not further penalised. The import relies on accurate incident timestamps in the source system.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Check incident counts (sev1/sev2 in YAML) vs notes field — do they match? Verify the MTTR value is plausible given the incident descriptions. A 0.7h MTTR for a P0 is suspicious — verify it wasn't measured from wrong timestamps.

what_it_measures: Minimum number of engineers whose combined commits account for ≥80% of total commits. A value of 1 means one person could leave and take 80%+ of the commit history with them — high single point of knowledge risk.
how_calculated: git log over trailing 6 months → count commits per author → sort by volume descending → count how many authors are needed to reach 80% of total commits. That count is the bus factor.
raw_data_inputs: Per-repo JSON → bus_factor.value and bus_factor.total_trailing_commits. Aggregated at product level by taking the median bus factor across active repos (weighted by trailing commit volume).
scoring_window: Trailing 6 months (not just current month — smoothed window)
null_behavior: Null if no commits in trailing 6 months. Redistributes its 30%.
known_limitations: Measures commit volume concentration, not knowledge concentration — an architect who writes lots of glue code raises the bus factor even if junior devs understand the system. Bot accounts inflate total commit counts (reducing the threshold) — bot filtering must be accurate. The 6-month trailing window means a recent team rotation takes months to be reflected. Aggregation across repos uses weighted median — a single large repo dominates the product score.
what_to_verify_in_qa: For repos with bus_factor=1 (flagged as WARN), verify it's not a bot account dominating commits. Check the per_contributor field in the JSON to see commit distribution. Small products — bus_factor=1 is structurally expected there.

what_it_measures: Percentage of top-level code modules (first directory level) that have been touched by more than one contributor. High score = no dark corners; low score = large swaths of code with only one person who's touched it.
how_calculated: git log over trailing 6 months with --name-only → group changed files by top-level directory → count modules with ≥2 distinct authors → percentage = multi_contributor_modules / total_modules × 100.
raw_data_inputs: Per-repo JSON → knowledge_distribution.percentage, .multi_contributor_modules, .total_modules. Aggregated at product level by weighted average across repos.
null_behavior: Null if no commits in trailing 6 months. Redistributes 30%.
known_limitations: Granularity is top-level directory only — if a repo puts everything under src/, every file is in the same 'module' and gets counted as one unit. Small repos with few modules can score 100% with just 2 engineers touching everything. The metric counts touch, not understanding — 2-line typo fixes count the same as architectural changes. Like bus_factor, this lags by up to 6 months.
what_to_verify_in_qa: Compare knowledge_distribution.total_modules against repo structure — very low module counts (1–3) can artificially inflate or deflate the score. A score of 100% with total_modules=1 means nothing.

what_it_measures: Percentage of commits or MRs that reference a JIRA ticket. Measures planning discipline — work that is traceable to a ticket is scoped, intentional, and auditable.
how_calculated: Manual input as a percentage (0–100). Could theoretically be auto-computed from ticket reference patterns in commit messages (same regex used for features_shipped fallback), but is currently manual to allow EM judgement on what counts.
null_behavior: Null for all months currently — new metric. Weight redistributes within Collaboration Quality to the other 3 metrics.
known_limitations: No data exists yet (component introduced 2026-04). Manual entry creates room for optimistic self-reporting. Auto-collection via commit regex would be more objective but requires accurate ticket pattern matching per product.
what_to_verify_in_qa: No data to verify yet — flag all as MISSING/new metric.

what_it_measures: Percentage of feature work items that had a written design/specification document created before coding began. Proxy for planning quality and reducing mid-sprint pivots.
how_calculated: Manual input as a percentage. EM estimates based on sprint planning records or Confluence doc timestamps vs. first commit dates.
null_behavior: Null for all months currently — new metric. Weight redistributes.
known_limitations: Highly subjective — 'spec' could mean anything from a Confluence page to a Slack message. No tooling enforces or measures this automatically. Risk of inflation in self-reporting.
what_to_verify_in_qa: No data to verify yet — flag all as MISSING/new metric.

what_it_measures: Median hours between requesting a cross-team code review and receiving a substantive response. Measures collaboration responsiveness — slow reviews create blocked engineers and batch-up dependencies.
how_calculated: Manual input in hours. EM estimates from GitLab MR review request timestamps or team feedback.
null_behavior: Null for all months — new metric. Weight redistributes.
known_limitations: Very difficult to measure without automated tooling. 'Cross-team' is ambiguous — within the same product pillar vs. across product pillars? No data exists yet.
what_to_verify_in_qa: No data to verify yet — flag all as MISSING/new metric.

what_it_measures: Percentage of feature PRs that include a documentation update alongside the code change. Measures documentation discipline — code shipped without docs creates long-term knowledge debt.
how_calculated: Manual input as a percentage. Could be partially auto-detected by checking if PRs touch doc/ or docs/ directories alongside code changes.
null_behavior: Null for all months — new metric. Weight redistributes.
known_limitations: Lowest weight (10%) in Collaboration Quality — least impactful metric. 'Documentation' is ambiguous (inline code comments? Confluence? README?). No data exists yet.
what_to_verify_in_qa: No data to verify yet — flag all as MISSING/new metric.
